title: Onsoo Botanicals — US market entry
decision_question: Should Onsoo enter the US market in 2027, and if so, by which route?

initial_hypothesis.statement: Enter the US in 2027 through an Amazon-led launch; add specialty retail from 2029 once proven.
initial_hypothesis.explanation: The evidence supports the CEO's route over the retail-led route, which breaks the investment cap and the group-margin floor. But Option A meets the four-year payback only if ACoS stays below about 28.6% — barely above the pilot's 28% and below the 32% scaling benchmark — and it reaches about $26M, not $40M, by 2030. A good answer keeps the hypothesis but adds gates and resets the $40M ambition; abandoning the US altogether is defensible only if argued from the payback risk, and adopting the retail-led route is not defensible.

key_insights.text: Amazon unit contribution before advertising is $10.72 (44.7% of price); after ads at the pilot's 28% ACoS it is $4.00 per unit. Retail contribution is $7.54 per unit before the large fixed retail costs.

Option B (retail-led) needs peak cumulative investment of about $20.8M even on the planning team's own 4.5 units/door/week (about $25.5M at the 2.6 newcomer median), above the $18M cap, never pays back by 2030, and pushes group operating margin to about 4.5% in 2027, below the 8% floor.

The 4.5 units/door/week assumption is the 'above 20% awareness' benchmark; Onsoo's awareness is 4% (9% among K-beauty buyers), where the median is 2.6 — below the retailer's 4.0 delisting threshold. Mooncrest's exit illustrates the risk.

Option A at the planning ACoS of 25% pays back in 2030 (cumulative $2.40M); at the pilot's 28% it only just pays back ($0.38M); at the 32% scaling benchmark it does not ($-2.32M). Break-even ACoS for payback by 2030 is about 28.6%. A tariff rise to 25% alone turns the pilot case negative ($-0.74M).

No option meets both the $40M ambition and the constraints: A reaches about $26.4M of 2030 revenue; B reaches about $37.6M but breaks the cap. The board has to trade the ambition against the constraints.
Peak investment for A is small ($2.4M at 28% ACoS; $3.9M in the combined downside), so the downside of trying A is bounded; group margin stays above 9%.

Option J (Japan) pays back in 2029 with cumulative $1.8M by 2030 and lower risk, but it is a small, slow-growing market (1.5% a year; Onsoo already holds 3.1%). It is a credible alternative for 2027 given the one-launch bandwidth constraint.

The pilot is not a novelty spike: monthly units nearly doubled (7,400 to 14,000; June run-rate about 168,000 units a year), 4.5 stars, and repeat of 29% is close to the 31% newcomer benchmark — but below Korea's 48%, so Korean repeat rates should not be assumed.

The 1.3× Amazon halo in Option B rests on a cross-brand correlation (0.71) that does not show retail causes Amazon sales: brands that are already successful win more doors (reverse causality / confounding). Without the halo, Option B is even worse.

required_calculations.text: Amazon per-unit contribution before and after advertising
required_calculations.expected: $10.72 before ads; $4.00 after ads at 28% ACoS

required_calculations.text: Option B cumulative cash / peak investment vs the $18M cap
Option A payback / cumulative cash by 2030, with sensitivity to ACoS (and ideally tariff)
required_calculations.tolerance: ±$0.5M; the qualitative pattern (payback only below ~28–29% ACoS) matters more than exact values

required_calculations.text: Group operating margin check for Option B in 2027
required_calculations.tolerance: any calculation showing it is below 8%

required_calculations.expected: CAGR 2021–25 17.3%, against 5.1% for all facial skincare; K-beauty share 14.7% in 2025

decision_relevant_evidence.text: Investment cap $18M, payback by end-2030, group margin ≥ 8%, one launch in 2027
Onsoo aided awareness 4% (9% among K-beauty buyers) vs sell-through benchmarks by awareness band
Retailer delists below 4.0 units per door per week after 12 months
Agency ACoS benchmark for scaling brands: median 32% vs planning assumption 25% and pilot 28%
61% of K-beauty buyers buy on Amazon most often; 38% discover on TikTok
Competitor histories (Mooncrest loss; Saebom success but two Amazon-first brands stalled below $5M)
Label complaint (Korean-only text) — a compliance and conversion fix before scaling
Definition of the $5.2B trade-press figure vs Table 1 skincare-only $3.6B

contradictory_evidence: The planning team's 25% ACoS vs the 32% scaling benchmark
The retailer's 4.5 units/door/week vs the 2.6 median at Onsoo's awareness
The $40M ambition vs the investment cap and margin floor
Saebom's success vs Gaon Lab and Yeoreum stalling (survivorship bias)
Board member's correlation memo vs what a correlation across brands can show

reasoning_traps.text: Sizing from the market ("K-beauty is $3.6B growing 17%; 1% share is $36M") instead of from channel economics
Accepting the 4.5 units/door/week or the 25% ACoS assumptions without checking them against the benchmarks
Using Saebom as proof that Amazon-first works (ignoring the two stalled brands) or Mooncrest as proof retail never works
Assuming Korean repeat rates (48%) or treating the pilot growth rate as permanent
Recommending retail-led to meet the $40M ambition while ignoring that it breaks the cap and the margin floor
Accepting the board member's correlation as proof that retail drives Amazon sales (the 1.3× halo)
Using the trade-press $5.2B (skincare + makeup + hair care) as the skincare market

key_tradeoffs.text: Ambition ($40M by 2030) vs investment cap, payback and margin floor
Speed/awareness of retail vs capital risk and delisting risk
US upside vs the safer, smaller Japan scale-up (one launch only in 2027)
Advertising intensity (growth) vs contribution and payback

plausible_recommendations.text: Enter through Amazon in 2027 with explicit gates (e.g. ACoS ≤ ~28%, repeat ≥ ~30%, label fix, tariff watch); add retail only when awareness supports ≥ 4 units/door/week; reset the $40M ambition or accept a later date.

Prioritise the Japan scale-up in 2027 and keep the cross-border Amazon listing as a low-cost US test — defensible if argued from payback risk and the one-launch constraint, with a clear trigger for a US launch later.
Amazon-led entry with a lower fixed-cost base (smaller team, slower brand spend) to protect payback — defensible if numbers are shown.
Enter the US 'because the market is large and growing' without channel economics.

defensibility_criteria: Compares the options on the board's own constraints (cap, payback, margin floor), not only on revenue
Tests the planning assumptions (ACoS, units per door) against the benchmarks in the pack
States what has to be true for the chosen route to pay back, and what would trigger a change
Acknowledges that the $40M ambition is not reachable within the constraints on the evidence given
